subject: Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data

messages.author: 650a95b7b389a6b5
messages.subject: Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data
parts:
Hi,

For logistic regression with two random effects on intercept, I have trouble to converge when data are sparse across the two random effects.


The model:  

//   logit (P.ijk) = gamma.i +alpha.j + beta %*% X.ijk      
                 
//                   gamma.i~ N (  0, var= sigma_sq_1 )  : random effect from gamma, i=1,2, ...I
                                                          
//                   alpha.j ~ N ( 0, var= sigma_sq_2 )  :random effect from alpha, j=1,2,...J

//                   For simulation,   sigma_sq_1=sigma_sq_2=0.2^2


Stan codes: 

 data  { 
          int <lower=1> D ;                // D: number of predictor variables including fixed intercept
          int <lower=0> N;                 // N: number of total observations
          int <lower=1> I;                 // number of unique A
          int <lower=1> J;                 // number of unique B

          int <lower=0, upper=1> y[N] ;    // Binary outcome
          int <lower=1, upper=I> ll[N];    //  Random effect A index vector
          int <lower=1, upper=J> ll_b[N];  //  Random effect B index vector 

          row_vector[D] x[N] ;             // Predictor matrix ,dim =N by D

          // Prior distributions
          vector [D] mu ;                 // beta  ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma)   ; try mu=zero vector
          matrix [D,D] Sigma  ;           // beta  ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma)   ; try Sigma=I(D, 10000)
          real <lower=0> a;                 //sigma_sq_1/sigma_sq_2 ~ inv_gamma(a, b)     ;  try a=0.001
          real <lower=0> b;                 //sigma_sq /sigma_sq_2 ~ inv_gamma(a, b)     ;  try b=0.001

   }


 parameters {
   real <lower=0> sigma_sq_1 ; // gamma.i~ N (  0, sigma_sq_1 )
         real <lower=0> sigma_sq_2 ; // alpha.j~ N (  0, sigma_sq_2 )
   
         vector [I] gamma;  
         vector [J] alpha;  
   vector [D] beta;
       
        }
model {       
         
          beta  ~ multi_normal(mu,Sigma);     // beta  ~ multi_normal_prec(mu,Omega);  Omega=inverse (Sigma) ;
         
          sigma_sq_1 ~ inv_gamma(a, b) ; 
          sigma_sq_2 ~ inv_gamma(a, b) ; 

         for (i in 1: I) {                              
              gamma[i] ~ normal (0, sqrt(sigma_sq_1));
          }

        for (j in 1: J) {                              
              alpha[j] ~ normal (0, sqrt(sigma_sq_2));
          }


         for (n in 1:N) {

          y[n] ~ bernoulli_logit (  x[n] * beta + gamma [ ll[n] ] + alpha [ ll_b[n]  ] );

         }


  }


The model converged when most n.ij >0.  For sparse data when most n.ij=0 , e.x. I=82, J=83 ,  total observation N=1156 , RStan converged on beta , but did not converge on sigma_sq_1/sigma_sq_2 based on 4 MCMC chains (burnin=10000, n.iter=15000 each  ). I also attached trace plots.


   #              mean     se_mean         sd         2.5%         25%        50%        75%     97.5%    n_eff     Rhat
#sigma_sq_1 0.03089220 0.002318893 0.03712577 0.0007567716 0.005269823 0.01750292 0.04241555 0.1338236 256.3243 1.006176
#sigma_sq_2 0.03191066 0.003075880 0.03776611 0.0006246300 0.005110067 0.01790998 0.04502797 0.1366208 150.7529 1.035034


Is there any additional modeling technique for sparse data? There is a section of "Missing data & partially known parameters" in Stan manual. Should I go this direction? 

Thanks a lot.

Lisa

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data
parts:
These models are tricky to estimate without informative priors
when data is sparse. The true posterior winds up being close to
the prior, so if you use a very diffuse "BUGS-like" prior such as
inv_gamma(0.001,0.001), or uniform(0,1000) or something like that,
you'll run into statistical problems as well as computational
ones. It's what Andrew calls "the Folk Theorem":

http://andrewgelman.com/2009/05/24/handy_statistic/

Why are you specifying Sigma as data rather than estimating it?
There are recommendations for priors and how to estimate it in
our manual chapter on regression. If you really want a fixed
diagonal covariance prior, then just use independent priors --- the
multivariate versions are computationally costly.

- Bob

P.S. Andrew --- Lisa's already using sd appropriately --- variance
is sampled inverse gamma and then the sqrt of variance used in the normal.

Hi,Bob:

#1. I will take your advice to use independent N(0,sd=100) for beta. Since random effects are focus, I use a simple distribution on beta.

#2 If the model is sensitive to prior, then as "the Folk Theorem" you pointed out, there is something wrong with the model. In real case, the sparse data could reflect limited spatial clusters between A and B. I am not sure how to incorporate this information into the model.

Thanks.

Lisa

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Hierarchical logistic regression on sparse data
parts:
> On Apr 7, 2015, at 3:13 PM, Lisa Mu <lisa...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi,Bob:
>
> #1. I will take your advice to use independent N(0,sd=100) for beta. Since random effects are focus, I use a simple distribution on beta.

My advice was just that it's quite a bit faster in terms of
computation to use this

theta ~ normal(0, sigma);

for theta of size N rather than the equivalent

theta ~ multi_normal(rep_vector(0, N),
sigma * diag_matrix(rep_vector(0,N)));

We recommend a value of sigma that matches the problem, not
one of the BUGS-style super-diffuse priors. This is what
Andrew calls "weakly informative", though there's not a precise
definition. For instance, if you expect your values of
theta to be roughly in (-1,1), then a normal(0,5) is "weakly
informative." If you go to normal(0,100), you might as well
just use an improper uniform prior. You can substitute a Cauchy
for the normal if you want to allow the occasional outlier.

> #2 If the model is sensitive to prior, then as "the Folk Theorem" you pointed out, there is something wrong with the model. In real case, the sparse data could reflect limited spatial clusters between A and B. I am not sure how to incorporate this information into the model.

All models are sensitive to the prior in some form or another
because it affects the form of the posterior. It's just a quantitative
matter of how much. Of course, with a fixed prior, more data will wash
out the prior.

If you actually have information about the problem (and almost
everyone does before they start), then you want to include it in
the prior or the likelihood.

Also, the folk theorem is heavily hedged in saying there *may* be
something wrong with your model. There are legitimate models that
are hard to compute.

- Bob
